title: Courage Week 1 Part 1
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona's talk highlights the importance of recognizing and embracing differences between men and women, rather than assuming absolute distinctions based on cultural norms or power structures. By acknowledging that these differences are shaped by environment and social conditioning, we can move beyond simplistic categorizations and cultivate a more nuanced understanding of individual strengths and weaknesses. This approach allows us to appreciate the unique qualities of each person, rather than trying to fit them into predetermined roles or expectations.

sentences.text: I'm going to speak for a little while now with the recorder on.
Brief interruptions are welcome.
We will be doing some discussion later on with the recorder turned off.
For quite a while there was a feeling of absence for me in the teachings, in that all of the teachings that we studied were from male teachers.
So we've got this opportunity now, with this book coming out with stories by and about female teachers.
In entering into that, I'd like to spend this evening exploring what our expectations are, what our understanding is, and how teachings from male and female teachers might be different.
The first question that I asked myself along those lines was, so what's the difference between men and women?
Does anybody think they know the difference between men and women?
We only have an hour and a half.
That's a really good point.
So I started looking at how teachings might be different, going back to how the brains of men and women are different.
Just starting with some basic physiology and neurobiology: relative to body mass, there is no difference between the size of men's brains and women's brains.
Interestingly, per volume of brain, men have more neurons than women, and per unit volume of brain, women have more synapse pathways than men.
That really makes sense.
And then, just throwing a few more interesting little brain differences at you: the right inferior parietal lobule is more developed in females.

This part of the brain is associated with selective attention and perception, the memory involved in understanding and manipulating spatial relationships, and the ability to sense relationships between body parts.
It is also related to the perception of our own affects, our feelings.
Whereas the left inferior parietal lobule is more developed in males, and this is involved in the perception of time and speed and the ability to mentally rotate 3D figures.
The frontal and temporal lobes are more developed in females, and they are involved in the manipulation of language.
Language processing occurs in both sides of the brain in women, but only in the left side of the brain in men.
There are some other statistical differences, some of which we are familiar with and some of which we are not.

I'm not sure how they measured this first one: women are noted as being more developed in human relations, in recognizing emotional overtones in others and in language, emotional and artistic expressiveness, aesthetic appreciation, verbal language, and carrying out detailed and pre-planned tasks.
Then the characteristics of empathy, verbal skills, social skills, and security seeking.
And as a newborn, speech understanding is greater in women.
Men then have higher scores in [unclear: "blind studies"] and independence, dominance, spatial and mathematical skills, rank-related aggression, and, as a newborn, spatial skills.

There are differences which aren't necessarily stronger or weaker, but just different ways that things are done in estimating time, judging the speed of things, carrying out mental mathematical calculations, orientation in space, and visualizing objects in three dimensions.

On a personal note, before I had started studying this, I had noted to people that when Diane and I go hiking, between the two of us, we'll go on a path and we'll be able to keep track pretty well of where we are.
But we do it differently.
Diane will remember that we passed this particular bush with the red berries on it, and she'll remember the name of it too.
Or that rock with the flat face on the one side and the point that sticks out.
Whereas I'd navigate in hiking by knowing, okay, we passed into the valley and then went up a wash a bit to the left and then over into the next watershed, down a little bit.

As it turns out, and this isn't just a random coincidence, it's maybe a little more profound than in other couples, but women generally are landmark oriented and men generally are more spatial relationship oriented.
Having said all of that, there are some huge super caveats to even examining this whole question.
One is that they're all statistical.
Of course, it's not that men are this way and women are that way.
A second is that they're non-causal.
We know human brains are plastic, and brain development is physically changing in response to the culture that we grow up in.
If there were no natural differences between men's and women's brains, growing up in a culture that treated men and women differently, the brains would grow to be different.
The third caveat is that there are very blurry lines between men and women.
We tend to think immediately of sexual organs, and even there, there are blurry lines.
Then take that to the whole rest of the body and the male and female characteristics.
And from there, go not just to the physical differences but to gender identification, which may or may not be associated with some of the physical characteristics.
So while it's not causal, there are still associations between the teachings and whether a teacher is male or female.
But those teachings are very much in response to both physical characteristics and the culture that we grow up in.
And the fifth super caveat that I have noted is that these Zen stories by and about women teachers still are uncovered and survived through a male-dominated power structure.
So it could be that it was only the ones that the male teachers wanted to survive that did.
In fact, there are some studies of historical records in China where, if we look at the writings of history, they will say that there were hardly any nuns existent during, say, the 10th century.
History going back says, well, that's why we don't have female ancestors.
And yet when they uncover the archaeological records of census data taken at the time, it's like, well, gee, 15% of the Buddhist practitioners are women.
So there's some obvious history being rewritten there.
I'd like to touch finally on some roles that, in surveying people, are traditionally recognized as being male and female.
Of course, child rearing is recognized as being a female role, and this can be said to extend into compassion generally.
Maybe there's something more to be studied there.
Hunting and fighting have evolved as a male role, which might be a reason for us to study women ancestors in and of itself.
And power has traditionally been a male role, right or wrong.

So even though most of what can be said in studying the differences between men and women is relative and not absolute fact, still, recognizing patterns in our thinking and speech can help us be aware of what we might be able to take from these teachings as we go forward.
Switching gears for a bit: in studying how a new exposure to the teachings of women ancestors can impact us, let's continue to work with the rest of the package of Buddhism.
For example, during the Wednesday evenings over the last few months, we've been studying the seven factors of awakening in the Dharma Talks.
We had just started to talk about the sixth factor, which is concentration, or samadhi, and I'd like to go into that a little deeper for a moment.
Tim had given us an analogy of a spotlight on a stage for analyzing different aspects of our mindfulness.
Mindfulness is what's in the spotlight, and concentration is what he likened to our holding the spotlight still on just one of the actors and not wandering it around a bit.
Regarding concentration, leading Vipassana teacher Christina Feldman identifies it as collected mind.
Concentration is one-pointedness, bare-bones attending to the chosen object of meditation, which for us is usually breathing, but there are a lot of other opportunities there.
It's a single-minded letting go of other factors such as investigation or broader mindfulness, investigation being one of the factors that Vipassana focuses on.
I want to pause at this point to remember that concentration is only one tool, only one of the seven factors of awakening.
A common error is to treat one factor of awakening as though it were enlightenment by itself, or to label concentration as good and therefore awareness of arising emotions such as frustration as bad.
So we work on tools, but we remember they're just tools.
Another Vipassana teacher, Sharon Salzberg, identifies samadhi, or concentration, as a lot of moments in a row, or moment-to-moment awareness that is not distorted by grasping, aversion, or delusion.
This teaching from a Vipassana teacher is very much aligned with the teachings of the early Zen ancestors.
We place a lot of merit on the first six ancestors in China, the sixth one being Huineng, who speaks of being unattached to characteristics, not thinking about conditions.
So concentration isn't just that you grab it and you keep going straight.
There is a fortitude of mind there that keeps coming back moment by moment.
